title: Evolution of botulinum neurotoxin serotype X proteases to induce inflammatory cell death in cancer cells - Nature Biotechnology
text:
Download PDF

AbstractTriggering protease-activated cell death is a promising strategy for cancer treatment. Here, we used phage-assisted evolution to reprogram botulinum neurotoxin serotype X proteases to cleave and activate procaspase-1 and gasdermin D, key effectors of inflammatory cell death. We also developed an efficient system to broadly characterize the substrate specificity of wild-type and evolved botulinum neurotoxin serotype X protease variants. Evolved proteases triggered robust cell death across multiple cancer cell lines. The gasdermin D-cleaving protease exclusively induced lytic death, whereas the procaspase-1-cleaving variant initiated both lytic and apoptotic cell death. To enable self-delivery into mammalian cells, we reconstitute evolved proteases with a native BoNT translocation domain, selectively killing cultured cancer cells while sparing non-cancerous cells. Expression of the evolved protease targeting caspase-1 reduced tumor growth in a highly drug-resistant tumor mouse model. These findings establish an evolving protease system to modulate inflammatory cell death and highlight the potential of BoNT proteases as programmable tools for targeted cancer therapy.

MainProgrammed cell death pathways are important mediators of health and disease. Dysregulation of these pathways is essential to supporting the uncontrolled proliferation of cancer cells1,2. Activation of programmed cell death pathways in cancer cells, particularly highly inflammatory and lytic cell death pathways such as pyroptosis, represents a promising cancer intervention. Pyroptosis is initiated by the cysteine protease caspase-1, which is activated via inflammasome assembly in response to pathogen- or damage-associated signals3,4. Once active, caspase-1 cleaves substrates such as pro-interleukin-1β (pro-IL-1β), pro-IL-18 and gasdermin D5,6. Following cleavage, gasdermin D forms membrane pores that lead to cell lysis and cytokine release, thereby stimulating an immune response7,8,9. Inducing pyroptosis in tumors has been shown to promote immune clearance10,11,12, and several small-molecule therapies targeting this pathway are approved chemotherapies13. Additional strategies, such as direct activation of gasdermin D14,15 or delivery of caspase-1 (ref. 16), have also been explored as potential cancer treatments.An alternative approach is to emulate natural inflammatory signaling via the delivery of reprogrammed proteases to catalyze the cleavage and activation of key protein mediators of pyroptosis, including caspase-1 and gasdermin D. Gasdermins can be cleaved and activated by a diverse array of other proteases in addition to caspase-1, including hematopoietic cell proteases (for example, granzymes, neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G)17 and bacterial virulence factors (for example, SpeB)18. In this broader context, the presence of an active protease in the cytosol acts as an endogenous danger signal that triggers lytic cell death and immune responses. Ideally, such an approach would also be compatible with cell-type-specific delivery into cancer cells and would offer tunable specificities and pharmacokinetics to enable precise control of lytic cell death in therapeutic settings. Botulinum neurotoxin (BoNT) proteases19,20 are in widespread clinical use and could be promising starting points for such a strategy in light of their catalytic mechanism, modular architecture21, intrinsic ability to self-deliver into target cells22 and demonstrated evolvability23,24,25.BoNTs are dichain toxins composed of a light chain protease and a heavy chain, which is further divided into two functional domains: an N-terminal translocation domain (HN) and a C-terminal receptor-binding domain (HC)21. BoNTs have been approved for diverse indications, including cosmetic procedures, movement disorders, chronic migraines, autonomic dysfunctions and ophthalmological conditions, by inducing paralysis in various muscles26. The modular architecture of BoNTs makes them attractive targets for protein engineering; heavy chain and light chain domains can be swapped among serotypes27, additional cargos can be appended28,29,30, and receptor specificity can be enhanced by modifying the HC domain31. Prior work has shown that some wild-type BoNTs can induce apoptosis in certain cancer cells32,33, and targeted delivery using nanobody fusions to the HC have enhanced self-delivery selectivity for specific cancer cell types30. Despite these promising advances, BoNT proteases have not yet been engineered to directly induce changes in cell state such as the induction of lytic cell death. Recent developments in phage-assisted continuous evolution (PACE)34 have substantially expanded our ability to generate bespoke proteases23,35,36, yielding evolved BoNT proteases that selectively cleave target proteins other than their native SNARE substrates23.Although PACE can select against the cleavage of researcher-defined off-target substrates, it does not explicitly select against the cleavage of other off-target proteins that an evolving protease may acquire the ability to process during evolution. Traditional proteomics-based methods, such as N-terminomics37,38,39 and proteomic identification of protease cleavage sites40, are well suited for global analyses of protease activity but can be low throughput and may lack the sensitivity to detect low-frequency, yet biologically perturbative, off-target cleavage events. Display technologies enable high-throughput screening of diverse randomized peptide libraries41 and human-proteome-derived libraries42,43 but typically require purified protease, which can pose challenges for unstable or difficult-to-express protease variants. We developed a sensitive, high-throughput, scalable system for profiling the cleavage activity of natural and evolved BoNT proteases on thousands of substrates simultaneously by adapting the genetic circuitry of PACE into a pooled activity-enrichment assay.Here we expand the functional repertoire of BoNTs by applying PACE to evolve BoNT serotype X (BoNT/X) proteases44,45,46,47 that cleave and activate procaspase-1 or gasdermin D. Targeting two key mediators of inflammatory cell death provides a strategy to modulate cancer cell fate. Using our substrate profiling method, we showed that the evolved proteases exhibit a highly altered cleavage profile compared to the starting wild-type BoNT/X protease. Next, we evaluated the proteases in cancer cells and demonstrated that the gasdermin D-cleaving variant induced lytic cell death in several cancer cell lines. Interestingly, the procaspase-1-cleaving protease triggered concurrent lytic and apoptotic cell death across multiple cancer types. Although evolved solely for procaspase-1 cleavage, we confirmed that the evolved protease acquired broader caspase-like activity and processed additional death pathway substrates including caspase substrates. Furthermore, both evolved proteases initiated cell death when reconstituted with BoNT’s HN domain, enabling self-delivery into cancer cells. Finally, the procaspase-1-cleaving protease significantly reduced tumor growth in the drug-resistant KPCY mouse pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma model.ResultsApplication of a PACE circuit for protease evolutionTo evolve proteases that cleave the cell death effectors procaspase-1 (Fig. 1a) and gasdermin D (Fig. 1b), we used a PACE circuit capable of reprogramming protease substrate specificity23. During positive selection, selection phage are modified to express the desired protease instead of gene III (gIII), a gene required for phage propagation35 (Fig. 1c). Host cells contain an accessory plasmid that encodes a protease-activated T7 RNA polymerase (RNAP), which transcribes gIII in response to protein cleavage, thereby linking phage propagation to protease activity. The T7 RNAP is fused to a catalytically disabled variant of T7 lysozyme, a natural inhibitor of T7 RNAP, via a cleavable linker containing the desired substrate. In the absence of protein cleavage, the high effective concentration of T7 lysozyme with respect to T7 RNAP ensures minimal RNAP activity. Cleavage liberates T7 lysozyme from being tethered to T7 RNAP, restoring RNAP activity. Selection stringency in PACE can be modulated by altering circuit parameters. For example, adjusting the ribosome binding site (RBS) strength48 upstream of gIII influences protein levels, while changing the promoter controlling expression of the RNAP–lysozyme fusion modulates the concentration of substrate available for proteolysis49. During negative selection (Fig. 1c), proteolysis liberates an orthogonal RNAP that expresses gIII-neg, a dominant-negative mutant of gIII50. The resulting gIII-neg impedes phage propagation by preventing detachment from the host membrane50. This dual-selection PACE circuit allows simultaneous selection for cleavage of a desired target protein and against cleavage of undesired off-target sequences.Fig. 1: Phage-assisted evolution of proteases to cleave cell death substrates.Full size imagea, Evolution of a procaspase-1-cleaving protease. Following cleavage, gasdermin D inserts itself into the cell membrane, resulting in cell lysis. PACE was used to evolve a protease to cleave the interdomain linker of gasdermin D to activate pyroptosis. c, Overview of the PACE circuit. MP, mutagenesis plasmid; POI, protein of interest; P, promoter.Evolution of procaspase-1-cleaving proteasesOur initial campaign targeted cleavage within the interdomain linker (IDL) of procaspase-1. Native procaspase-1 undergoes autoproteolytic cleavage at several positions within the IDL to promote activation5,51. We first established a starting point for evolution by comparing the IDL of procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) to a 17-amino-acid segment of the endogenous substrate of BoNT/X, vesicle-associated membrane protein 1 (VAMP1), positions 56–72. One alignment (Fig. 2a) placed the cleavage site of VAMP1 (between Arg 68 and Ala 69) at an autoproteolytic cleavage site of procaspase-1 (between Asp 316 and Ala 317). Wild-type BoNT/X with various substrates at a 1:1 ratio was generally too toxic for these experiments and was thus excluded.Using this alignment, we identified a series of intermediate protein sequences to serve as evolutionary stepping-stones between VAMP1 and procaspase-1. We generally prioritize the most challenging specificity or activity changes early in the evolutionary process when the wild-type enzyme has the highest folding energy reserves to accommodate the impact of mutations that arise during evolution36. We found that the VAMP1-Asp70Ile mutation reduced cleavage by BoNT/X protease and was therefore selected as the first evolutionary stepping-stone (PC_SS1 hereafter; Fig. 2a and Extended Data Figs. 1 and 2a–c).Having defined the initial evolutionary stepping-stone, we next implemented protease PACE positive selection to evolve BoNT/X toward procaspase-1 recognition (Fig. 2b and Extended Data Fig. 1). PACE for 72 h on PC_SS1 evolved several mutations conserved among PACE clones: Thr167Ala, Pro174Leu and Ser240Asn (Supplementary Table 1). These mutations cluster near the BoNT/X protease substrate-binding groove, with Thr167Ala positioned close to the scissile bond. We characterized protease variants first with a luminescence reporter that uses the positive selection circuit to express luciferase from the T7 promoter. Evolved proteases X(SS1)a, X(SS1)b and X(SS1)c demonstrated proteolytic activity on PC_SS1 (Extended Data Fig. 2d) but showed no activity on the second procaspase stepping-stone PC_SS2 (Extended Data Fig. 2e).The pooled phage output surviving PACE on PC_SS1 was next subjected to phage-assisted non-continuous evolution (PANCE)52,53,54 on PC_SS2, which contained six additional mutations toward procaspase-1 (Fig. 2a,b, Extended Data Fig. 1 and Supplementary Table 1). PANCE, which uses serial, rather than continuous, dilution, is less stringent than PACE and therefore provides evolving gene populations a greater opportunity to access a solution that survives selection before being diluted out of the lagoon52. Although Thr167Ala, Pro174Leu and Ser240Asn mutations were retained during PANCE on PC_SS2, additional conserved mutations emerged, including Asn144Ile, Ala218Val and Tyr314Ser (Supplementary Table 1). Variants such as X(SS2)a, X(SS2)c, X(SS2)f and X(SS2)g exhibited moderate activity on PC_SS2 while retaining activity on VAMP1 and PC_SS1, with no detected activity on procaspase-1 in the luminescence assay (Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). These results suggest that even though PANCE on PC_SS2 yielded active proteases, and PC_SS2 shares >50% homology with procaspase-1, additional evolution is necessary to evolve activity on the procaspase-1 substrate.Subsequent evolution campaigns selected directly for cleavage of procaspase-1 (residues 304–320; Fig. 2a,b). First, PANCE on a low-stringency positive selection circuit yielded proteases X(PC1)c, X(PC1)d and X(PC1)e, which showed weak activity on procaspase-1 and residual activity on VAMP1, PC_SS1 and PC_SS2 (Fig. 2c,d and Extended Data Fig. 2c–e). To increase activity, we transitioned to PACE using a more stringent circuit, replacing the T7 RNAP promoter with the weaker T3′ RNAP promoter50 and adjusting RBS strength in front of gIII to reduce transcriptional activation following RNAP liberation (Extended Data Fig. 1). To accommodate these adjustments, the 17-residue procaspase-1 substrate was placed in the linker between T3′ RNAP and the inhibitor T7 lysozyme; while the T3′ RNAP variant has high selectivity for the T3 promoter, it remains effectively inhibited by T7 lysozyme23. After several passages, protease variants X(PC2)a–X(PC2)e demonstrated substantial activity on procaspase-1 (Fig. 2c), with enriched mutations such as Asp161Asn, Asn164Lys, Asn235Ile, Ser279Pro and Ser280Pro likely contributing to this gain (Supplementary Table 1). Residual activity on VAMP1 (residues 28–88), however, highlighted the need for negative selection (Extended Data Fig. 2c).Phage surviving procaspase-1 positive selection PACE were therefore subjected to dual-selection PACE, incorporating positive selection for procaspase-1 and negative selection against VAMP1. Proteases emerging from the first round of dual selection, including X(PC3)a and X(PC3)c, showed decreased activity on VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c). In a second round of dual selection, proteases were evolved under a more stringent selection that lowered the amount of available positive selection substrate and increased the concentration of gIII-neg (Extended Data Fig. 1). Resulting variants, X(PC4)a–X(PC4)d, were less active on procaspase-1 than X(PC2) and X(PC3) proteases, but were highly selective for procaspase-1 cleavage (Fig. 2c), losing all detected activity on VAMP1 and PC_SS1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). Overall, these findings indicate that phage-assisted evolution successfully reprogrammed wild-type BoNT/X to cleave procaspase-1 while eliminating any detected activity on its native substrate VAMP1.In vitro characterization of procaspase-1-cleaving proteasesWe selected X(PC4)c, hereafter referred to as X(PC), from the final round of dual-selection PACE for detailed analysis due to its robust expression and ease of purification (see Fig. 2d for sequence). We compared the activity of wild-type BoNT/X and X(PC) on fusion proteins containing the targeted regions of either procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) or VAMP1 (residues 28–88), inserted between maltose-binding protein (MBP) and glutathione S-transferase (GST) proteins to facilitate bacterial expression and purification of these substrates. As expected, wild-type BoNT/X cleaved the VAMP1 fusion but showed no detectable activity on the procaspase-1 substrate (Extended Data Fig. 3a). By contrast, X(PC) selectively cleaved the procaspase-1 substrate with no activity on VAMP1 (Extended Data Fig. 3a). These data confirm that X(PC) retains selective activity on procaspase-1 and has lost its ability to cleave its native substrate when tested in purified protein assays.We quantified the kinetic parameters of X(PC) to validate the selectivity suggested by luciferase activity and assess how evolution impacted catalytic efficiency. Using a previously reported fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET)-based assay23 (Fig. 2e,f), we determined that X(PC) cleaving procaspase-1 has a Km of 4.05 µM, a kcat of 0.423 s−1 and a kcat/Km (catalytic efficiency) of 0.104 s−1 µM−1. Despite undergoing negative selection only on VAMP1, X(PC) also lost activity on all other known native BoNT/X substrates, including VAMP4, VAMP5 and YKT6 (Fig. 2e). Using the same FRET-based assay, we compared the activity of X(PC) to that of wild-type BoNT/X protease on its native substrate VAMP1 (Km = 6.93 µM, kcat = 3.52 s−1, kcat / Km = 0.508 s−1 µM−1; Fig. 2e,f). X(PC) on procaspase-1 is only fivefold slower than wild-type BoNT/X protease on VAMP1. These findings highlight that PACE can reprogram substrate specificity with high selectivity, rather than merely broaden protease promiscuity.We previously observed that BoNT proteases can evolve to cleave a target substrate at a peptide bond that differs from the anticipated cleavage site23. Indeed, mass spectrometry revealed that cleavage by X(PC) occurred between Glu 314 and Asp 315 rather than the predicted site between Asp 316 and Ala 317 inferred from its alignment with VAMP1 (Fig. 2a). Luminescence-based activity assays suggest that this cleavage site shift evolved during higher-stringency rounds of selection on procaspase-1. Early variants from low-stringency selection on procaspase-1 (X(PC1)a–X(PC1)c) showed little activity on procaspase-1 but retained activity on PC_SS1 and VAMP1. By contrast, variants from higher-stringency campaigns (X(PC2)a–X(PC2)e) evolved strong activity on procaspase-1, maintained activity on VAMP1 but lost activity on PC_SS1 (Extended Data Fig. 2c,d). These observations suggest that as stringency increased, evolving proteases selected for a P2′ aspartic acid preference, a feature present at the observed cleavage sites in both VAMP1 and procaspase-1, but absent in PC_SS1 (Fig. 2a).Characterization of procaspase-1 cleavage in mammalian cellsTo determine whether X(PC) can cleave full-length procaspase-1 in a cellular context, we transfected hemagglutinin (HA)-tagged procaspase-1-Cys285Ala into HEK293T cells and incubated lysates with decreasing doses of purified proteases (Extended Data Fig. 3b). The Cys285Ala substitution renders procaspase-1 catalytically inactive, preventing toxicity in HEK293T cells. Whereas BoNT/X showed no activity, X(PC) cleaved procaspase-1-Cys285Ala (Extended Data Fig. 3b). These findings demonstrate that X(PC) can cleave full-length procaspase-1 in protein lysates even though it was evolved on only a 17-amino-acid substrate fragment, procaspase-1 (residues 304–320).Next, we determined if X(PC) remains functional when expressed intracellularly in mammalian cells. HEK293T cells were co-transfected with HA-tagged X(PC) and Flag-tagged procaspase-1-Cys285Ala, and protease activity was assessed by immunoblotting (Fig. 2g). In cells expressing procaspase-1-Cys285Ala, X(PC) generated a distinct cleavage product at the expected molecular weight corresponding to procaspase-1 cleavage. Together, these results demonstrate that X(PC) remains catalytically active when expressed in mammalian cells and can cleave full-length procaspase-1 even in the presence of the endogenous intracellular human proteome.Evolving procaspase-1-cleaving proteases with reduced off-target cleavage activityAlthough X(PC) demonstrated high selectivity for procaspase-1 over VAMP1, its transfection into mammalian cells lacking procaspase-1 (HEK293T cells) still resulted in reduced cell viability compared to a catalytically inactive X(PC) variant, consistent with residual off-target activity (Extended Data Fig. 3c). To determine how this off-target activity may have changed during directed evolution, we transfected wild-type BoNT/X protease at the same concentration. Notably, BoNT/X was approximately tenfold more toxic than X(PC) in this cell line, as measured by CellTiter-Glo assay 48 h after transfection (Extended Data Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 1). While this toxicity may reflect the promiscuity of BoNT/X compared to other serotypes, it is also possible that BoNT/X cleaves an unidentified host protein essential to HEK293T survival44,45.To understand the nature of X(PC)’s off-target cleavage activity more deeply, we began by investigating cleavage of downstream caspase-1 substrates and observed that X(PC) likely cleaved IL-1β (Fig. 2h, Extended Data Fig. 2f and Extended Data Fig. 3d,e) at a position distinct from caspase-1 cleavage events following Asp 26 and Asp 116. Based on a sequence alignment between procaspase-1 and IL-1β (Fig. 2a), and observed cleavage product sizes (Fig. 2h), we hypothesized that X(PC) cleaves IL-1β in the flexible N-terminal region of the protein between Glu 18 and Asp 19. We also identified ORC1 based on P2–P4′ homology to procaspase-1 (Extended Data Fig. 2b) and noted that evolved variants also cleaved ORC1 (residues 691–707) in the luminescence assay (Extended Data Fig. 2g). Thus, although negative selection against VAMP1 reduces cleavage on SNARE targets, evolution on procaspase-1 appears to confer caspase-like substrate preferences that include IL-1β or substrates with complete homology to the P2–P4′ of procaspase-1 such as ORC1 (residues 691–707).As this region of ORC1 cleaved by X(PC4) variants occurs in a section of the protein predicted to be structured and therefore may be less accessible to a protease, we prioritized eliminating cleavage of IL-1β by performing evolution using dual-selection PANCE with a 25-amino-acid segment from IL-1β as the negative selection substrate, IL-1β (residues 5–29; Fig. 2a). Variants X(PC5)a–X(PC5)c emerged with mutations, including a shift of Thr167Ala to Thr167Ser (Supplementary Table 1). In luminescence activity profiling, these variants retained comparable activity on the procaspase-1 (residues 304–320) substrate used for evolution as X(PC), but showed no cleavage of IL-1β (residues 5–29) or ORC1 (residues 691–707; Fig. 2c and Extended Data Fig. 2b–g). These results confirm that dual-selection strategies can further reduce off-target cleavage while maintaining desired target cleavage activity within the PACE environment.We next tested the ability of X(PC5) variants to cleave full-length proteins in HEK293T cells by co-transfecting plasmids expressing either procaspase-1-Cys285Ala or IL-1β, along with evolved proteases (Fig. 2g). Variants X(PC5)a and X(PC5)b showed partial cleavage of full-length procaspase-1, whereas X(PC5)c showed no detectable activity. Cleavage of full-length IL-1β was not detected in all three cases (Fig. 2h). While these results demonstrate that further negative selection reduced off-target cleavage, all three variants performed worse than X(PC) at cleaving full-length procaspase-1 in mammalian cells. Western blots suggest that the reduced cleavage by X(PC5) variants likely stems from lower expression and stability of the proteases in mammalian cells (Fig. 2g).Substrate specificity profiling of natural and evolved proteasesTo assess the substrate preferences of a protease in a broad and rapid manner, we developed a method for profiling protease activity on a substrate library by adapting the PACE selection circuit. We reasoned that replacing the T7 RNAP-transcribed gIII cassette with a chloramphenicol resistance gene would enable the selective enrichment of bacterial cells that express substrates cleaved by a protease of interest when challenged with antibiotic (Fig. 3a). We could express a protease of interest under an inducible promoter and select in the presence of chloramphenicol in Escherichia coli expressing a large library of peptide substrates present in the linker between T7 RNAP and its fused T7 lysozyme inhibitor. Note, proteins are labeled with their UniProt entry names.Validation experiments established that cells expressing T7 RNAP–linker–T7 lysozyme fusions containing various substrate sequences exhibited growth rates in the presence of chloramphenicol that correlate with the protease’s known activity on that substrate (Supplementary Fig. 2a,b), demonstrating the potential of this strategy to serve as a protease substrate profiling method. Similar to eukaryotic systems such as YESS-NGS55, this bacterial approach offers the ability to profile natural and evolved proteases in parallel on thousands of natural and synthetic substrates through high-throughput sequencing without requiring protein purification.As an initial application of the method, we generated a library of all possible single-residue substitutions to a 60-mer VAMP1 sequence and assessed the cleavage activities of wild-type BoNT/X and BoNT/F proteases on this library (Extended Data Fig. 4a and Supplementary Fig. 2c–f). We found that BoNT/X exhibits a substantially greater tolerance for substitutions in the native substrate sequence than BoNT/F. BoNT/X protease cleaves VAMP1 between Arg 68 and Ala 69, and notable de-enrichment at Ala 69 and Asp 70, along with slight de-enrichment at Arg 68 in the substrate profile, suggests that P1, P1′ and P2′ primarily dictate BoNT/X protease substrate recognition (Fig. 3b and Extended Data Fig. 4a). The protease appears particularly selective at the P1′ position, tolerating only cysteine, glycine, serine or the wild-type residue alanine. Notably, the P11 position, corresponding to Arg 58 in VAMP1, slightly de-enriches most amino acids aside from arginine, suggesting that P11 may participate in an important exosite contact (Extended Data Fig. 4a). Beyond these key positions, BoNT/X protease exhibits tolerance to mutations, which may contribute to its broad SNARE substrate range44,45. By contrast, BoNT/F light chain, when profiled on VAMP1 (Supplementary Fig. 2c), exhibited greater selectivity. BoNT/F protease cleaves between Gln 60 and Lys 61, with stringent amino acid preferences at multiple positions surrounding the cleavage site. These findings are consistent with previous reports that BoNT/F light chain cleaves only VAMP1, VAMP2 and VAMP3, while BoNT/X cleaves VAMP1 through VAMP5 as well as YKT6 (refs. 44,45). These findings also support our observation that BoNT/X protease causes toxicity in HEK293T cells, likely due to cleavage of additional, unidentified substrates (Supplementary Fig. 1).After confirming that X(PC)’s activity in the selection circuit correlates with its to luminescence-detected protease activity (Supplementary Fig. 3a), we performed a similar analysis on proteases evolved to cleave procaspase-1 using a library of all possible single-residue substitutions of a 17-mer substrate sequence (Fig. 3a). Compared to wild-type BoNT/X protease, both X(PC2)b, an earlier evolutionary intermediate with activity on both VAMP1 and procaspase-1, and X(PC) demonstrated more stringent substrate requirements (Fig. 3b,c and Supplementary Fig. 3b–d). X(PC), which cleaves procaspase-1 between Glu 314 and Asp 315, displayed strict specificity at positions P3, P2, P1, P1′, P2′ and P3′ (Fig. 3c and Supplementary Fig. 3e).Next, we sought to identify combinations of substitutions in the procaspase-1 substrate that could be cleaved by our evolved proteases. X(PC) shows selectivity for residues at six amino acids within the procaspase-1 substrate sequence from P3 to P3′ (Fig. 3c). Testing all possible combinations of these residues would require a library of 109 sequences, above the limits of our high-throughput sequencing readout. Their catalytic activity enables rapid remodeling of cellular pathways, and their substrate specificity offers a route to precisely rewire signaling networks. Despite these advantages, therapeutic proteases, including all currently approved BoNT drugs26, remain limited in scope, with most clinical applications relying on native enzymes acting on endogenous substrates20. Expanding their use requires the ability to reprogram protease specificity to cleave targets with functional consequences for cell fate.Here we advance and apply a generalizable system for evolving programmable proteases using BoNT/X protease and PACE. Focusing on cell death, a process tightly governed by proteolysis, we evolved proteases capable of initiating lytic cell death. The evolved BoNT/X proteases cleave either procaspase-1 or gasdermin D, driving potent cytotoxicity in cancer cells. These proteases function as self-delivering agents when reconstituted with the BoNT translocation domain, enabling intracellular activity without the need for additional delivery vectors.Notably, X(PC) and X(GD) exhibit distinct cell death phenotypes and kinetic profiles, demonstrating that evolved proteases can drive different outcomes depending on their chosen target and biochemical properties. Whereas X(GD) mediates an exclusively lytic execution program, X(PC) initiates concurrent lytic and apoptotic cell death. Although we confirmed that X(PC) successfully drives pyroptosis through direct caspase activation in specific contexts such as SUP-B15 cells, canonical pyroptosis is a highly regulated process that often requires multiple coordinated signals. The resistance or mixed cell death phenotypes observed in other target-expressing cell lines likely reflect an absence of these requisite contextual signals. In such environments, the broader substrate reactivity of X(PC) overcomes this biological bottleneck by triggering a complex cell death program consistent with PANoptosis, rather than isolated canonical cleavage events.To understand evolved protease substrate specificity more comprehensively, we developed a substrate compatibility profiling system that maps substrate preferences and nominates potential off-target substrates across the human proteome. We anticipate that this tool will prove useful for both therapeutic design and understanding on-target versus off-target effects in reprogrammed proteases.Notably, although X(PC) targets many proteins within caspase-driven pathways, it often cleaves them at noncanonical sites. For example, X(PC) cleaves the inflammatory cytokine pro-IL-1β between Glu 18 and Asp 19, distinct from the canonical caspase-1 sites at Asp 26 and Asp 116. Similarly, X(PC) cleaves ATG3 and numerous other caspase substrates identified in the MerCASBA database within 30 amino acids of their native cleavage sites. This noncanonical processing may either mimic caspase activity or yield unintended consequences by destroying effector domains or native caspase motifs. An important next step toward enhancing the specificity of these evolved proteases is characterizing the cleavage fragments of off-target substrates and further rounds of negative selection against relevant off-targets. Although our initial substrate profiling and TMT-TAILS data provide a foundation for understanding the specificity of variants like X(PC), defining their therapeutic relevance will require additional safety assessments. Future studies comparing the global off-target and toxicity profiles of these self-delivering proteases head-to-head with established small-molecule inducers of pyroptosis and apoptosis will help inform their therapeutic potential.Our findings also highlight a specificity–activity trade-off during directed evolution. While stringent negative selection yielded the highly specific X(PC5) variants, it simultaneously attenuated their expression, stability and overall cleavage efficiency in mammalian cells. Although the current catalytic efficiency of X(PC) is sufficient to slow tumor growth in vivo in the highly treatment-resistant KPCY model, advancing these enzymes for broader systemic use will require overcoming this evolutionary bottleneck to maximize both potency and selectivity. Future optimization paths may benefit from integrating artificial intelligence-driven computational protein design to reinforce the BoNT protease scaffold75. A more stable scaffold would better tolerate the structurally disruptive mutations often required for substrate recognition and may allow simultaneous access to variants with both the high selectivity seen in the X(PC5) series and the robust intracellular activity of X(PC).Although we achieved effective protease activity and self-delivery in cancer cells in cell culture, BoNT holotoxins are naturally restricted to neuronal targeting due to the specificities of their receptor-binding domains. Overcoming this limitation will be critical to fully realizing the potential of BoNT-delivered proteases for in vivo applications. In this study, we established in vivo efficacy through a doxycycline-inducible X(PC) cell line. Recent advances have demonstrated the feasibility of replacing BoNT receptor-binding domains with nanobodies to redirect specificity toward cancer-relevant surface markers, although the efficiency of such an architecture has not been confirmed in vivo30. We envision further improvements through directed evolution of the receptor-binding domain to recognize additional receptors or tumor-specific antigens. Advancements in targeted delivery could also mitigate systemic toxicity that may result from off-target protease cleavage.Together, our findings establish a versatile strategy for evolving proteases that cleave non-native, therapeutically relevant targets and reprogram cellular behavior.
